notes: "Kala Nag pulled up his post." The post appears for the first time here, so a young reader may not know what it is. Optional fix: add "Kala Nag stood by a post." to the sentence where the boy sleeps near him.

Grammar stays in present and past simple. The plot order matches Kipling: the rope in the pen, the joke, the night walk, the dance, the proof on the hill, the new name. All three quiz keys are correct and unambiguous.
"Big Toomai had a son of ten, Little Toomai." This is a little stiff. "Big Toomai had a ten-year-old son called Little Toomai" reads more naturally (taste only).
"Elephants dance in secret places, but nobody ever sees them." This is acceptable in present simple. "them" could refer to the places or the elephants, but either reading makes sense.

"At a word from him, the great elephant lifted him gently onto his back." Both "him"s refer to the boy, which is clear enough. "At a word from the boy, the great elephant lifted him..." would be smoother.
There are no conditionals and no passives. Machua Appa's line in the present perfect matches quiz 3, which paraphrases it in the past simple. That is acceptable.

Faithful details: Black Toomai, the grandfather who saw the capture, the great-grandfather's name, ten feet at the shoulder, the old joke meaning "never", and the clearing that grew wider. The quiz keys are correct and each has only one defensible answer.

"Hearing the boy's name, Kala Nag curled his trunk round Little Toomai ... Petersen Sahib, who had noticed that the elephant obeyed the child, asked him why he had taught Kala Nag such a trick." In this scene the boy gives no command, so 'obeyed the child' is only loosely motivated. Optional fix: "At a whispered word from Little Toomai, Kala Nag curled his trunk round him...".
"With the first gray light" uses American spelling, while the rest of the text uses British forms ('round'). Consider "grey" for consistency.
The prose is literary rather than padded. It carries Kipling's images: the carrot pulled from soft earth, counting to ten over and over, the salute given only to the greatest of men.

summary: All five levels retell Kipling's 'Toomai of the Elephants' faithfully: the rope in the keddah, Petersen Sahib's 'when you have seen the elephants dance' joke, the night dance, the trampled clearing, Machua Appa's verdict and the new name with the elephants' salute. Grammar fits each level, the quiz keys are correct, and the content is gentle enough for 4+. Only minor stylistic notes remain.
